**PRODUCTION SAFETY MANUAL**
**Version 4.2**
**Issued: April 15, 2025**
**Next Review: July 15, 2025**

**Prepared by:** Theo Marsh, Safety & Training Coordinator
**Owner:** Production Safety Department
**Distribution:** All crew members, department heads, and production office staff. Keep a copy in the production office and on the call board at all times.

---

**CHANGELOG**

Superseded versions (3.9 and earlier) are archived in the production office. Do not use prior versions for compliance.

---

**1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE**

This manual establishes the minimum safety standards and operational procedures for all personnel working on productions under the jurisdiction of the Safety Department. It applies to all stages of production: pre-production, principal photography, and wrap.

The training manual states that Production Safety Manual v4.2 version is 4.2. Record status: current. This is the current controlled version. Any printed copy is uncontrolled once distributed; verify you are using the latest version on the shared drive before relying on it.

The guidelines herein are not a substitute for good judgment. When a situation presents a hazard not covered by this manual, stop work and consult your department head or the Safety Coordinator. When in doubt, ask.

**2. GENERAL SAFETY PRINCIPLES**

2.1 **Everyone is responsible for safety.** It is not the job of one department alone. If you see a condition that could cause harm, correct it if you are trained to do so, or report it immediately to your AD or the Safety Coordinator.

2.2 **Stop Work Authority.** Every crew member has the authority and the responsibility to stop work in the case of an imminent danger. The work does not resume until the hazard is mitigated.

2.3 **No task is so urgent that it cannot be done safely.** This includes the final shot of the day. Rushing causes accidents.

2.4 **Report all incidents and near misses.** An incident includes any injury, illness, or damage to equipment or property. A near miss is any event that could have caused harm but did not. Reporting a near miss is not an admission of fault; it is a tool for prevention. Use the Incident/Near-Miss Report form (Form S-4, available on the call board and in the production office). Reports must be submitted within 24 hours of the event.

2.5 **Housekeeping.** Keep walkways, stairwells, and exits clear of cables, grip equipment, and personal items. Trip hazards are the most common cause of on-set injuries. Clean up spills immediately. Dispose of all waste in designated receptacles.

2.6 **Fatigue management.** Long hours are part of the industry, but fatigue is a hazard. Take your breaks as scheduled. Do not operate heavy equipment or drive vehicles if you are too tired to do so safely. Notify your supervisor if you feel unsafe due to fatigue.

2.7 **Drugs and alcohol.** Possession or use of illegal drugs or alcohol on set or in the workplace is prohibited. Prescription medications that may impair judgment must be reported to the Safety Coordinator for a confidential assessment.

**3. EMERGENCY PROCEDURES**

3.1 **Emergency Contacts** (posted on the call board and inside the production office door)

| Contact | Number |
|---------|--------|
| Emergency Services (Fire/Police/Ambulance) | 911 |
| Set Medic (on-location) | See daily call sheet |
| Safety Coordinator (Theo Marsh) | Ext. 4217 |
| Production Office | Ext. 4200 |
| Studio Security (if on lot) | Ext. 4311 |
3.2 **Evacuation.** When the alarm sounds, or when directed by the AD or Safety Coordinator, stop work immediately and proceed to the nearest designated assembly point. Assembly points are marked on the location map posted with the daily call sheet. Do not use elevators. Do not return to the work area for personal belongings. Department heads are responsible for a head count of their crew and must report any missing personnel to the AD at the assembly point.

3.3 **Fire.** If you discover a fire, sound the alarm and call 911. If the fire is small and you are trained to use a fire extinguisher, you may attempt to extinguish it. Otherwise, evacuate. Know the location of the nearest fire extinguisher in your work area. Extinguishers are inspected monthly by the Safety Coordinator; do not block access to them.

3.4 **Severe Weather.** In the event of a tornado warning, lightning within 10 miles of the location, or other severe weather, the AD will call a stop to outdoor work. Take shelter in the designated safe area. For lightning, the rule is 30/30: if the time between the flash and the thunder is less than 30 seconds, seek shelter, and do not resume outdoor work until 30 minutes after the last flash. Do not stand under tall objects or near metal rigging.

3.5 **Medical Emergency.** For any medical emergency, call 911 and then contact the Set Medic. Do not move an injured person unless they are in immediate danger. Provide first aid only if you are trained to do so. If an ambulance is called, one crew member should be assigned to direct them to the location.

3.6 **Active Threat / Hostile Situation.** If you see an armed person or other active threat, evacuate if it is safe to do so. If you cannot evacuate, hide, lock or barricade the door, and silence your phone. Call 911 when it is safe. Do not attempt to confront the individual.

**4. EQUIPMENT HANDLING**

4.1 **General.** All equipment must be operated only by trained and authorized personnel. Read the manufacturer's manual before operating unfamiliar equipment. Never operate equipment that is damaged or malfunctioning; tag it out of service and report it to your supervisor.

4.2 **Lifting.** Use proper lifting technique: bend at the knees, keep your back straight, and lift with your legs. For loads over 50 lbs, use a two-person lift or mechanical assistance. Do not attempt to lift beyond your capability.

4.3 **Cables and Power.** Do not run cables across walkways without protecting them with cable ramps or mats. Check all power cords for frayed insulation or exposed wires before use. Only use grounded outlets and extension cords rated for the load. Do not overload circuits. All power distribution must be done by a qualified electrician.

4.4 **Ladders and Lifts.** Inspect ladders before use; do not use a ladder with broken rungs or missing feet. Place ladders on a firm, level surface. Maintain three points of contact when climbing. Do not stand on the top two rungs of a ladder. Scissor lifts and boom lifts may only be operated by certified operators. Harnesses must be worn and attached when working in a lift basket.

4.5 **Weapons and Props.** All prop weapons, including firearms, replicas, and airsoft guns, must be checked by the Armorer or Prop Master before use. Never point a weapon at anyone, even if you believe it is unloaded. Weapons must be stored in a locked container when not in use. Live ammunition is never permitted on set.
**Appendix A: Safety Bulletin #14 (Current Version)**
**Subject:** Heat Illness Prevention and Hydration
**Bulletin No.:** 14
**Issued:** 6/2/25
**Supersedes:** Bulletin No. 11 (issued 5/15/24)
**Distribution:** All crew, all departments

Heat illness is a serious and preventable risk on outdoor shoots and in unconditioned interiors. This bulletin updates the previous guidance and is effective immediately.

**A.1 Responsibilities**

- **Key Grip / Grip Department:** Provide shade structures (pop-ups, canopies) at base camp and near any outdoor work area where feasible. Ensure a supply of ice is available for cooling towels and water.
- **Assistant Director (AD) Department:** Schedule regular rest breaks in shaded or air-conditioned areas. Monitor the crew for signs of heat illness and adjust the shooting schedule if conditions warrant.
- **Production / Craft Services:** Maintain a supply of water and electrolyte replacement drinks at all times. Water must be potable and cool. Do not rely solely on crew members to bring their own water.
- **Each Crew Member:** Drink water every 15–20 minutes, even if you do not feel thirsty. Wear light-colored, loose-fitting clothing and a hat when working in direct sun. Report any symptoms of heat illness to your supervisor immediately.

**A.2 Symptoms to Watch For**

- **Heat Cramps:** Muscle spasms, often in the legs or abdomen.
- **Heat Exhaustion:** Heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, headache, cool and clammy skin.
- **Heat Stroke (Medical Emergency):** Hot, dry skin (no sweating), confusion, altered mental state, seizures, or loss of consciousness.

**A.3 Emergency Response**

If a crew member shows signs of heat stroke, call 911 immediately. While waiting for help, move the person to a cool area, remove excess clothing, and apply cool water or ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin. Do not give fluids to a person who is confused or unconscious.

**A.4 Work/Rest Cycles (High Heat Conditions)**

When the heat index is 90°F or higher, the AD will implement a work/rest cycle. A typical cycle is 45 minutes of work followed by 15 minutes of rest in a cool area. The AD may shorten work periods or extend rest periods based on conditions and crew feedback.

**PRODUCTION SAFETY MANUAL**
**Version 4.2**
**Issued: April 15, 2025**
**Next Review: July 15, 2025**

**Prepared by:** Theo Marsh, Safety & Training Coordinator
**Owner:** Production Safety Department
**Distribution:** All crew members, department heads, and production office staff. Keep a copy in the production office and on the call board at all times.

---

**CHANGELOG**

Superseded versions (3.9 and earlier) are archived in the production office. Do not use prior versions for compliance.

---

**1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE**

This manual establishes the minimum safety standards and operational procedures for all personnel working on productions under the jurisdiction of the Safety Department. It applies to all stages of production: pre-production, principal photography, and wrap.

The training manual states that Production Safety Manual v4.2 version is 4.2. Record status: current. This is the current controlled version. Any printed copy is uncontrolled once distributed; verify you are using the latest version on the shared drive before relying on it.

The guidelines herein are not a substitute for good judgment. When a situation presents a hazard not covered by this manual, stop work and consult your department head or the Safety Coordinator. When in doubt, ask.

**2. GENERAL SAFETY PRINCIPLES**

2.1 **Everyone is responsible for safety.** It is not the job of one department alone. If you see a condition that could cause harm, correct it if you are trained to do so, or report it immediately to your AD or the Safety Coordinator.

2.2 **Stop Work Authority.** Every crew member has the authority and the responsibility to stop work in the case of an imminent danger. The work does not resume until the hazard is mitigated.

2.3 **No task is so urgent that it cannot be done safely.** This includes the final shot of the day. Rushing causes accidents.

2.4 **Report all incidents and near misses.** An incident includes any injury, illness, or damage to equipment or property. A near miss is any event that could have caused harm but did not. Reporting a near miss is not an admission of fault; it is a tool for prevention. Use the Incident/Near-Miss Report form (Form S-4, available on the call board and in the production office). Reports must be submitted within 24 hours of the event.

2.5 **Housekeeping.** Keep walkways, stairwells, and exits clear of cables, grip equipment, and personal items. Trip hazards are the most common cause of on-set injuries. Clean up spills immediately. Dispose of all waste in designated receptacles.

2.6 **Fatigue management.** Long hours are part of the industry, but fatigue is a hazard. Take your breaks as scheduled. Do not operate heavy equipment or drive vehicles if you are too tired to do so safely. Notify your supervisor if you feel unsafe due to fatigue.

2.7 **Drugs and alcohol.** Possession or use of illegal drugs or alcohol on set or in the workplace is prohibited. Prescription medications that may impair judgment must be reported to the Safety Coordinator for a confidential assessment.

**3. EMERGENCY PROCEDURES**

3.1 **Emergency Contacts** (posted on the call board and inside the production office door)

| Contact | Number |
|---------|--------|
| Emergency Services (Fire/Police/Ambulance) | 911 |
| Set Medic (on-location) | See daily call sheet |
| Safety Coordinator (Theo Marsh) | Ext. 4217 |
| Production Office | Ext. 4200 |
| Studio Security (if on lot) | Ext. 4311 |

documents.content:
3.2 **Evacuation.** When the alarm sounds, or when directed by the AD or Safety Coordinator, stop work immediately and proceed to the nearest designated assembly point. Assembly points are marked on the location map posted with the daily call sheet. Do not use elevators. Do not return to the work area for personal belongings. Department heads are responsible for a head count of their crew and must report any missing personnel to the AD at the assembly point.

3.3 **Fire.** If you discover a fire, sound the alarm and call 911. If the fire is small and you are trained to use a fire extinguisher, you may attempt to extinguish it. Otherwise, evacuate. Know the location of the nearest fire extinguisher in your work area. Extinguishers are inspected monthly by the Safety Coordinator; do not block access to them.

3.4 **Severe Weather.** In the event of a tornado warning, lightning within 10 miles of the location, or other severe weather, the AD will call a stop to outdoor work. Take shelter in the designated safe area. For lightning, the rule is 30/30: if the time between the flash and the thunder is less than 30 seconds, seek shelter, and do not resume outdoor work until 30 minutes after the last flash. Do not stand under tall objects or near metal rigging.

3.5 **Medical Emergency.** For any medical emergency, call 911 and then contact the Set Medic. Do not move an injured person unless they are in immediate danger. Provide first aid only if you are trained to do so. If an ambulance is called, one crew member should be assigned to direct them to the location.

3.6 **Active Threat / Hostile Situation.** If you see an armed person or other active threat, evacuate if it is safe to do so. If you cannot evacuate, hide, lock or barricade the door, and silence your phone. Call 911 when it is safe. Do not attempt to confront the individual.

**4. EQUIPMENT HANDLING**

4.1 **General.** All equipment must be operated only by trained and authorized personnel. Read the manufacturer's manual before operating unfamiliar equipment. Never operate equipment that is damaged or malfunctioning; tag it out of service and report it to your supervisor.

4.2 **Lifting.** Use proper lifting technique: bend at the knees, keep your back straight, and lift with your legs. For loads over 50 lbs, use a two-person lift or mechanical assistance. Do not attempt to lift beyond your capability.

4.3 **Cables and Power.** Do not run cables across walkways without protecting them with cable ramps or mats. Check all power cords for frayed insulation or exposed wires before use. Only use grounded outlets and extension cords rated for the load. Do not overload circuits. All power distribution must be done by a qualified electrician.

4.4 **Ladders and Lifts.** Inspect ladders before use; do not use a ladder with broken rungs or missing feet. Place ladders on a firm, level surface. Maintain three points of contact when climbing. Do not stand on the top two rungs of a ladder. Scissor lifts and boom lifts may only be operated by certified operators. Harnesses must be worn and attached when working in a lift basket.

4.5 **Weapons and Props.** All prop weapons, including firearms, replicas, and airsoft guns, must be checked by the Armorer or Prop Master before use. Never point a weapon at anyone, even if you believe it is unloaded. Weapons must be stored in a locked container when not in use. Live ammunition is never permitted on set.

**Appendix A: Safety Bulletin #14 (Current Version)**
**Subject:** Heat Illness Prevention and Hydration
**Bulletin No.:** 14
**Issued:** 6/2/25
**Supersedes:** Bulletin No. 11 (issued 5/15/24)
**Distribution:** All crew, all departments

Heat illness is a serious and preventable risk on outdoor shoots and in unconditioned interiors. This bulletin updates the previous guidance and is effective immediately.

**A.1 Responsibilities**

- **Key Grip / Grip Department:** Provide shade structures (pop-ups, canopies) at base camp and near any outdoor work area where feasible. Ensure a supply of ice is available for cooling towels and water.
- **Assistant Director (AD) Department:** Schedule regular rest breaks in shaded or air-conditioned areas. Monitor the crew for signs of heat illness and adjust the shooting schedule if conditions warrant.
- **Production / Craft Services:** Maintain a supply of water and electrolyte replacement drinks at all times. Water must be potable and cool. Do not rely solely on crew members to bring their own water.
- **Each Crew Member:** Drink water every 15–20 minutes, even if you do not feel thirsty. Wear light-colored, loose-fitting clothing and a hat when working in direct sun. Report any symptoms of heat illness to your supervisor immediately.

**A.2 Symptoms to Watch For**

- **Heat Cramps:** Muscle spasms, often in the legs or abdomen.
- **Heat Exhaustion:** Heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, headache, cool and clammy skin.
- **Heat Stroke (Medical Emergency):** Hot, dry skin (no sweating), confusion, altered mental state, seizures, or loss of consciousness.

**A.3 Emergency Response**

If a crew member shows signs of heat stroke, call 911 immediately. While waiting for help, move the person to a cool area, remove excess clothing, and apply cool water or ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin. Do not give fluids to a person who is confused or unconscious.

**A.4 Work/Rest Cycles (High Heat Conditions)**

When the heat index is 90°F or higher, the AD will implement a work/rest cycle. A typical cycle is 45 minutes of work followed by 15 minutes of rest in a cool area. The AD may shorten work periods or extend rest periods based on conditions and crew feedback.
